title: priority-routing-blackout-sim-debrief
body:
Purpose:
Run a controlled simulation of a region-level control-plane blackout to validate priority-based routing, DNS failover behavior, and our traffic-shift orchestration. This document captures the run notes, anomalies observed, and recommended follow-ups. Draft — working notes for the SRE on-call and networking teams.

Summary of simulation (what we did):
- Window: 2026-02-28 02:00–03:00 UTC (scheduled maintenance slot).
- Scenario: Simulated abrupt control-plane/network isolation of us-east-1 (primary) for the inference control-plane (API gateway and regional routing). Data plane in other regions (us-west-2, eu-west-1) remained healthy.
- Mechanism: We emulated a regional outage by deploying a simulated ACL on the regional frontend LB that dropped control-plane traffic and toggled a health-check failure in the region load balancer. No customer data was altered.
- Objectives: Verify GSLB / DNS priority routing fallback, TTL behavior, edge caching interactions, and automated traffic-shift runbook steps.

Goals / Success criteria:
- DNS-based failover should move >95% of new connections away from us-east-1 within two TTL cycles.
- In-flight requests should see acceptable latency degradation (p95 increase < 200ms) and error rate <2% during the shift window.
- KV-cache warm-up time in target region should be <60s for typical prompt shapes.
- Automated rollback should function if error rate or latency exceed thresholds.

Pre-reqs and pre-checks (what we ran before starting):
- Reduced global DNS TTL for api.redwood-inference.com from 60s -> 15s (72h prior) and verified via dig.
- Ran smoke tests against each region (success rate >99.8%).
- Verified canary endpoints and routing rules in GSLB and Layer 7 routing (weights, priorities).
- Ensured runbook sigchain: on-call SRE, network lead, product on-call, and SOC were paged.

Run steps executed (actual sequence):
1) At T0 (02:00 UTC) — mark us-east-1 control-plane as unhealthy via lb-health toggle (simulated outage).
2) Trigger: GSLB should demote primary priority for us-east and raise weights for us-west-2 and eu-west-1.
3) Observe DNS answers with dig +short @8.8.8.8 api.redwood-inference.com and curl -v to /health endpoints.
4) If weighted shift <90% after 2 TTLs, execute manual weight update in GSLB console.
5) If client error rate >2% for 5m, enable gradual traffic mirroring to alternative region to accelerate cache warming.
6) Monitor automated rollback triggers (latency, error rate).

Commands used (representative):
- dig +short @8.8.8.8 api.redwood-inference.com || true
- kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=edge-gateway || true
- curl -s -D - https://api.redwood-inference.com/health | head -n 20 || true
- gcloud dns record-sets transaction start --zone=redwood-gslb || true
- aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes --target-group-arn <arn> --attributes Key=stickiness.enabled,Value=false || true
(Notes: we used internal automation for weight changes, not manual CLI in prod).

Observed outcomes (metrics and anomalies):
- DNS: After TTL=15s, the percentage of clients resolving to us-east dropped to 8% after 30s and 2% after 60s (success for DNS demotion).
- Latency: p50 stable, p95 increased from 95ms -> 240ms during the first 90s of shift (peak), then leveled to ~170ms after caches warmed.
- Error rate: baseline 0.2% -> spike to 3.8% for ~4 minutes. Primary cause: a subset of long-polling websocket connections that retried aggressively and overloaded the new region's ingress.
- KV cache: miss rate rose 10x initially; median KV fetch latency to remote store increased by ~80ms until cold cache warmed (approx 45s).
- Observability gaps: Our traffic-split dashboard showed a 25s lag in evaluating region-specific token-cost metrics, meaning we didn't immediately detect cost impact during the first minute.
- Rollback: Automated rollback did not trigger because error rate returned below threshold after 5 minutes. Manual intervention was not required.
- Unexpected: A small set of legacy clients pinned to A records with longer TTLs (~5min) continued sending ~1.5% of traffic to us-east even after demotion.

Post-sim analysis (why things happened):
- DNS performed as expected for new resolvers, but older resolvers (and cached A records hard-coded in some client versions) caused residual traffic.
- The websocket-heavy clients with aggressive reconnect behavior caused a transient overload in the accepting region due to connection churn. We lack per-client backoff enforcement at the edge.
- Cache warm-up time was within our target but KV misses amplified error surfaces since some internal fallbacks assume regional data locality.
- Observability lag prevented real-time cost analysis — this needs improvement for tight SLAs.

Immediate remediation actions (short-term, owner, ETA):
- Implement temporary throttling/backoff rules for websocket reconnects at edge layer (owner: Luis Romero, ETA: 2026-03-12).
- Create a mitigation playbook item to manually update GSLB weighted records for long-TTL clients (owner: Maya Chen, ETA: 2026-03-01).
- Add health-check header propagation to improve routing decisions and trace region of origin in requests (owner: Priya Nair, ETA: 2026-03-08).

Medium-term improvements (owner, proposal):
- Add client-version telemetry to detect hard-coded A-records and notify product teams to ship fixes or instruct customers (owner: eng-sre & product-hosted-api, proposal due 2026-04-01).
- Implement graceful connection handoff for long-lived connections (websockets) using session drain + redirect pattern (owner: serving-runtime, proposal due 2026-04-15).
- Shorten our global DNS default TTL for public endpoints to 30s with a phased rollout and client communication (owner: network, ETA: 2026-04-10).

Observability / runbook updates required:
- Add a dedicated traffic-shift dashboard that shows region split, p50/p95 latency per region, KV-cache hit ratio, and websocket connection churn in <10s refresh windows. (owner: observability, ETA: 2026-03-20).
- Add a pre-shift checklist item: verify ability to modify GSLB weights programmatically via API keys and that runbook operator has keys available. (owner: eng-sre, ETA: 2026-03-05).

Unresolved questions / risks:
- How many external clients still have hard-coded A records vs. DNS caching behavior? Need a sampling study.
- Is session affinity required for any internal enterprise customers that would break if we shift region? Inventory needed.
- Do we want to invest in active DNS poisoning-resistant approaches (multi-proxy approach) vs. faster orchestration of BGP/Anycast? Cost/complexity tradeoff.

Notes for next simulation (runbook tweaks):
- Include a small synthetic websocket client population that accurately models reconnect/backoff behavior.
- Run the shift during higher traffic volumes (simulate ramp) to validate auto-throttles.
- Add a step to intentionally inject a long-TTL DNS client to measure residual traffic.

Appendix (raw event log snippets):
- 02:00:12 UTC — health-check toggled for us-east: HC=FAIL
- 02:00:28 UTC — first dig shows resolver answers: [us-west-2, us-west-2, eu-west-1] (weighted)
- 02:01:05 UTC — p95 latency spike 240ms (graph ref: CONFLUENCE-1234/graphs)
- 02:04:12 UTC — error rate back to baseline 0.24%

References and links:
- Confluence simulation plan: CONFLUENCE-1234
- Runbook skeleton and prior tests: JIRA-SRE-987
- Infra PR that updated GSLB automation: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/412

Action items (short checklist):
- [ ] Luis: deploy websocket backoff rule (2026-03-12)
- [ ] Maya: publish manual weight-update instructions for long-TTL clients (2026-03-01)
- [ ] Observability: create traffic-shift dashboard (2026-03-20)
- [ ] Product: inventory of clients with session affinity (2026-03-15)

Comments / notes to self:
- This felt like a realistic failure mode. DNS did the heavy lifting for new connections, but we still rely on several non-DNS mechanisms (client behavior, session affinity) that complicate full-region failover. Next sim should focus on websocket-heavy flows and client-side TTL noncompliance.

Draft status and next steps:
- Sharing with network and product on-call for review. After addressing immediate remediation items, schedule a follow-up simulation that injects long-lived connection churn and long-TTL clients.
